subtype: Approach: one-on-one conversations before the group meeting [Action]
passage: Before the Thursday meeting, Tanvir spent Tuesday and Wednesday having tea, one person at a time, with the leads who disagreed about the new leave-tracking tool for the Bengaluru office. With Farida from HR he learned the worry wasn't the tool itself but a promise she had made to managers of a report by March. With the payroll lead he heard the fear of entering everything twice. Two disputes turned out to be misunderstandings: payroll thought HR wanted to replace their sheet, while HR only wanted to read it. Tanvir sent each a short message: 'Here's what I heard. Is that right?' By Thursday morning the loud disagreement had shrunk to one real question, about the launch date. The meeting took twenty minutes.

qa.q: How long did the meeting take?

qa.a: Farida was worried about keeping the promise she had made to managers of a report by March.

qa.q: What could Tanvir do if a private talk showed a real conflict?
qa.a: Tanvir could bring the two sides together with a one-page list of options and agreed criteria, since a real difference needs a fair way to decide.

qa.q: How might the payroll lead have felt before Tanvir's chat?
qa.a: They likely felt threatened, fearing double entry and believing HR wanted to replace their sheet.

grounding: Shows a lead talking privately with each stakeholder and finding that two of the conflicts were misunderstandings that vanished before the full meeting.

subtype: Approach: one-on-one conversations before the group meeting [Action]
passage:
'Thanks for making time before Thursday, Nilesh,' Rukmini said, closing the cabin door. 'I wanted to hear your side before the big meeting.'
'My side is simple. The new app will add work for my warehouse staff. They'll have to scan every box twice.'
'Twice? Where did you hear that?'
'At the demo last month.'
Rukmini opened her laptop. 'That was the old version. Now it's one scan, and it replaces the paper form they fill today.'
Nilesh leaned in and read. 'So it's actually less work?'
'For your team, yes. What else worries you?'
'Training time. We're short-staffed in November.'
'Then we train in October. I'll put that in the plan.'
Nilesh laughed. 'I came in ready to fight on Thursday.'
'That's why I wanted to talk today.'

qa.q: Where had Nilesh heard about scanning every box twice?
How did Nilesh feel coming into the talk, and how did it change?
qa.a: Nilesh came in defensive and ready to fight, then felt relieved and even amused on seeing it was less work.

qa.q: What else could Rukmini do before the Thursday meeting?
qa.a: She could have similar private talks with each other stakeholder, so any other misunderstandings are cleared before the group meets.

qa.q: How might Nilesh's warehouse staff be affected?
qa.a: They will scan once instead of filling paper forms, and train in October before the busy November.

grounding: It shows a lead talking privately with a stakeholder before the group meeting and finding the conflict was a misunderstanding that disappears.

subtype: Approach: one-on-one conversations before the group meeting [Action]
passage:
I'm Vinita, and before the budget meeting last quarter I did something that felt slow: I met each of the four department heads alone, twenty minutes each, two days before.
Sharmila from marketing surprised me most. In emails she had been fighting the new reporting tool. Alone, with a cup of tea, she said her real fear was that it would expose how little her campaigns were tracked. 'I'm not against it. I'm scared of looking bad.' We agreed she would get two weeks to clean up her data before any dashboards were shared.
Operations had thought the tool meant layoffs. It didn't. I told them so, plainly.
By Thursday, two of the three conflicts I'd dreaded were gone. The meeting took forty minutes. People looked almost bored. I was delighted.

qa.q: How long did Vinita meet each department head for?
qa.a: Twenty minutes each, two days before the meeting.

qa.q: What was Sharmila really feeling about the tool?
qa.a: Sharmila was scared of looking bad, worried the tool would show how little her campaigns were tracked.

qa.q: Why did the private meetings work better than debating in the group meeting?
qa.a: In private, people could say their real fears, which turned out to be misunderstandings that could be fixed before Thursday.

qa.q: How might Operations have felt on hearing the tool didn't mean layoffs?
qa.a: Operations would likely feel relieved and more open to the tool, having feared for their jobs.

grounding: It shows a lead meeting each stakeholder privately before the group meeting and finding that most conflicts were misunderstandings.
